content.intro: This lesson covers Variables and Immutability. It sits in Module 3, Rust Syntax and Primitive Data Types, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Variables and Immutability matters when you work with unsafe invariants and external contracts. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Unsafe Rust permits a narrow set of operations whose safety obligations the compiler cannot fully prove. Every unsafe boundary needs explicit invariants, valid initialization, correct aliasing, and compatible external contracts.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Variables and Immutability, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Bindings are immutable unless declared mut; shadowing creates a new binding. Prefer explicit conversions and clear formatting over silently assuming a numeric conversion is safe.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Variables and Immutability guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
